parts.title: Part I – Multiple Choice Questions
parts.instructions: This examination paper contains 100 multiple choice questions only. You must answer all of them. Each question carries one point. There is only one best answer for each question; blacken the letter of your choice on the Scantron answer sheet with a pencil. Constants that you may require for questions 71-100 (table printed on p.15 after Q70): g = 10 m/s², c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s (light in air and free space), refractive index of air n(air) ≈ 1, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s, sin 30° = cos 60° = 0.50, sin 45° = cos 45° = 0.71.

All answers were solved independently; every calculation (main items and similar questions) is checked in tools/src_matric/general_science_2023/verify_calcs.py. Biology items are checked against the Eritrean MoE Biology textbooks G9–12, chemistry items against the Chemistry textbooks G9–12, physics items against the Physics textbooks G9–12; each textbook ref names its series in 'subject' and was keyword-checked in the extracted text (verified_in_text). There is no General Science textbook. See confidence and review_flag on each question.

questions.stem: Organelles such as plant chloroplast can only be observed under
explanation_steps: Textbook (G9 p.7): 'An electron microscope examines smaller structures such as viruses or the internal structures of cells ... An electron microscope helps to identify organelles like ribosomes, chromosomes or chloroplasts.'

C is keyed as the textbook answer. Note that whole chloroplasts (green dots) can be seen with a good light (compound) microscope; their internal structure (grana, thylakoids) needs an electron microscope, so the word 'only' makes the item imprecise.
tips: Light microscope: cells, nuclei, chloroplasts as green dots. Electron microscope: ribosomes, membranes, internal structure of organelles, viruses.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following can be seen only with an electron microscope?
explanation_steps: Viruses (about 20–300 nm) are far below the resolution of a light microscope. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.section: 1.1.3 Tools of biology – the electron microscope
textbook_ref.subject: Biology

questions.review_flag: Keyed C from the textbook (EM identifies chloroplasts), but chloroplasts are visible under a light/compound microscope (B/E); 'can only be observed' is scientifically too strong. Teacher to decide.

questions.stem: The ______ is the fluid region of a cell.
explanation_steps: The cytoplasm is the jelly-like fluid (cytosol) between the cell membrane and the nucleus, in which the organelles are suspended (G9 p.12).
Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: The organelle that controls all the activities of the cell is the
explanation_steps: The nucleus contains the DNA and controls cell activities. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Bacteria attach to solid surfaces by their
explanation_steps: Textbook (G9 p.29): 'Pili are short, fine, hair-like appendages that are thinner than flagella and may serve as a means of attachment to solid surfaces.'
Flagella are used for swimming. Answer: B.

similar_questions.stem: The long whip-like structures that help bacteria to swim are
explanation_steps: Flagella rotate to move the bacterium. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Bacterial capsule is composed of
explanation_steps: Textbook (G9 p.29): 'Some bacteria have a polysaccharide layer, called a capsule, which surrounds the cell membrane.' It protects the cell from the host's immune defences and helps attachment.
Peptidoglycan makes the bacterial cell wall; cellulose makes plant cell walls. Answer: D.

similar_questions.stem: The bacterial cell wall is made mainly of
explanation_steps: Peptidoglycan distinguishes bacterial walls from plant (cellulose) and fungal (chitin) walls. Answer: C.

questions.stem: The category genus is subdivided into
explanation_steps: Ranks from highest to lowest: kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species (G9 p.54).
A genus is divided into species. Answer: D. (Family is the rank above genus.)

similar_questions.stem: Several related families make up a(n)
explanation_steps: Families are grouped into orders. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.section: 2.1 The importance of classification – levels of classification
textbook_ref.subject: Biology

questions.stem: Rust fungi
explanation_steps: Textbook (G9 p.81): fungus-induced plant diseases cause tremendous economic losses in agriculture; 'Rust fungus belongs to the basidiomycota group. There are more than 250 rust fungi that attack crop cereals, such as wheat, barley, and oats.'
So A, B, C and D are all true. Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: Blight fungus, which attacks potatoes and tomatoes, belongs to
explanation_steps: The textbook places blight fungus in zygomycota. Answer: C.

questions.stem: The parasitic protozoa, class sporozoa, have locomotory structures known as
explanation_steps: Textbook (G9 p.70): 'Sporozoa: members of this group are almost all parasites. They are spore-forming protists without a locomotory structure' (e.g. Plasmodium).
Cilia – ciliophora (Paramecium); flagella – mastigophora (Trypanosoma); pseudopodia – sarcodina (Amoeba). Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: Which protozoan causes malaria?
explanation_steps: Plasmodium, a sporozoan transmitted by the female Anopheles mosquito. Answer: C.

questions.stem: One of the following is true of RNA.

options.E: It has identical nucleotides with DNA.

explanation_steps: RNA is made from a DNA template by transcription (G12 pp.4–12).

RNA is usually single-stranded (not a double helix), carries genetic information (mRNA carries the code) and has ribose and uracil instead of deoxyribose and thymine, so its nucleotides differ from DNA's. Answer: C.

similar_questions.stem: Which base is found in RNA but not in DNA?
explanation_steps: RNA has uracil in place of thymine. Answer: E.

questions.stem: Cell organelle which is found only in animal cell is
explanation_steps: Textbook (G9 p.14): 'Centrioles – these are barrel-shaped organelles found only in animal cells.'
Plastids and cell walls are found only in plant cells; the Golgi apparatus and protoplasm occur in both. Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is found in plant cells but not in animal cells?
explanation_steps: Chloroplasts (plastids) occur only in plant and algal cells. Answer: C.

questions.stem: The most primitive vascular plants are
explanation_steps: Mosses (bryophytes) are non-vascular; ferns (pteridophytes) are the simplest seedless vascular plants with true roots, stems and leaves (G9 p.83).
Cycads (gymnosperms) and maize (angiosperm) are seed plants, more advanced; kelps are algae. Answer: D.

similar_questions.stem: Which group of plants has seeds that are not enclosed in a fruit?
explanation_steps: Gymnosperm = 'naked seed' (e.g. pines, cycads). Answer: C.

questions.stem: All are true of plasmolysis, except
explanation_steps: Textbook (G9 p.23): in a hypertonic solution water leaves the cell (plasmolysis). 'In a plant cell, the cell membrane shrinks and separates from the cell wall. In an animal cell, the cell shrinks and collapses, as there is no cell wall.'
The rigid cell wall does not shrink, so B is false. E is also false: bursting happens in a hypotonic solution, not in plasmolysis. B is keyed; E is also accepted.
A and C are textbook statements, and D (the collapsed animal cell dies) is consistent with 'shrinks and collapses'.
tips: Hypertonic → shrink (plasmolysis/crenation); hypotonic → swell (plant cell turgid, animal cell bursts).

similar_questions.stem: A plant cell placed in pure water becomes
explanation_steps: Water enters by osmosis; the wall resists bursting, so the cell becomes turgid. Answer: C.

questions.review_flag: Two options are false for plasmolysis: B (the cell wall does not shrink) and E (animal cells burst only in hypotonic solutions). B keyed, E accepted. Teacher to decide.

questions.stem: Succulent plants like "Cactus" modify their leaves to spine in order to
explanation_steps: Xerophytes such as cacti reduce their leaves to spines, which greatly reduces the surface for transpiration and so reduces water loss (G9 p.143); water is stored in the fleshy stem, and the green stem photosynthesises.
Answer: A. (Spines also protect against grazing animals.)

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT an adaptation of xerophytes?

options.D: Large thin leaves with many stomata

explanation_steps: Large thin leaves would lose much water; xerophytes have small leaves or spines. Answer: D.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 4 – Plants, Animals and the Environment
textbook_ref.section: 4.2 Adaptations of plants to water – xerophytes
textbook_ref.subject: Biology

questions.stem: An organism adapted to a saline environment is called
explanation_steps: Halophytes are plants adapted to salty (saline) soils or water, e.g. mangroves on the Red Sea coast (G9 p.147).
Xerophytes – dry habitats; hydrophytes – water; epiphytes grow on other plants. Answer: D.

similar_questions.stem: Mangrove trees on the Red Sea coast have roots that grow upward out of the mud to
explanation_steps: Breathing roots (pneumatophores) take in air because the waterlogged mud has little oxygen. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 4 – Plants, Animals and the Environment
textbook_ref.subject: Biology

questions.stem: Which of the following is the first enzyme to mix with food?
explanation_steps: Digestion begins in the mouth, where saliva adds salivary amylase (ptyalin), which starts breaking starch into maltose (G10 p.33).
Pepsin acts later in the stomach, trypsin and maltase in the small intestine; humans do not make cellulase. Answer: B.

similar_questions.stem: Pepsin digests
explanation_steps: Pepsin is a protease active in the acidic stomach. Answer: B.

questions.stem: The use of mucous secreted by the stomach is to

options.A: protect the lining of the stomach.
options.B: kill the germs in the food.

explanation_steps: Mucus coats the stomach wall and protects it from being digested by pepsin and damaged by hydrochloric acid (G10 pp.34–35).
HCl kills germs; pepsin digests protein. Answer: A.

similar_questions.stem: Which substance in gastric juice kills bacteria in food?
explanation_steps: The strongly acidic HCl kills most microorganisms. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following is incorrect of polysaccharides?

options.A: They can be stored in the body.

explanation_steps: Polysaccharides (starch, glycogen, cellulose) are large molecules: insoluble in water, not sweet, suitable for storage (glycogen in liver and muscle) and hydrolysed by enzymes such as amylase (G9 p.120; G10 p.5).
So 'They are soluble in water' is incorrect. Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: Which carbohydrate is a storage polysaccharide in animals?
explanation_steps: Glycogen is stored in the liver and muscles. Answer: C.

additional_textbook_refs.unit: Unit 3 – Metabolic Processes and Energy Transfers in Living Organisms
additional_textbook_refs.subject: Biology

questions.stem: One of the following is incorrect about red blood cells. They are
explanation_steps: Mature red blood cells are biconcave, have no nucleus (so they cannot divide), are made in the red bone marrow and are flexible/elastic, so they can squeeze through narrow capillaries (G10 p.67).
They are not rigid. Answer: A.

similar_questions.stem: Why do mature human red blood cells have no nucleus?

options.B: To make room for more haemoglobin

explanation_steps: Without a nucleus there is more space for haemoglobin to carry oxygen. Answer: B.

questions.stem: One of the following cannot be antigenic if transferred to a person.
explanation_steps: An antigen is a foreign substance that stimulates the immune system to produce antibodies (G10 pp.77–79). The immune system recognises the body's own ('self') tissues and does not attack them.
Foreign tissue, mismatched blood, foreign cells and bacteria are all antigenic. Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: Antibodies are produced by
explanation_steps: B-lymphocytes (plasma cells) produce antibodies. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.section: 4.1 The immune system – antigens and antibodies
textbook_ref.subject: Biology

questions.stem: The type of immunity children acquire when they get infection from neighbours is
explanation_steps: Natural active immunity develops when the body makes its own antibodies after catching an infection naturally (G10 p.106).
Passive natural = antibodies from the mother (placenta, breast milk); active artificial = vaccination. Answer: A.

similar_questions.stem: A baby receives antibodies from its mother's milk. This is
explanation_steps: Ready-made antibodies received naturally = natural passive immunity. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Energy production through aerobic cellular respiration does not need the presence of
explanation_steps: Aerobic respiration: food (glucose; also fats and proteins) + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O + energy (ATP) (G9 p.131).
Carbohydrates, fats and proteins can all be fuels and oxygen is essential; carbon dioxide is a product, not a requirement. Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: Where in the cell does most aerobic respiration take place?
explanation_steps: The Krebs cycle and electron transport chain occur in the mitochondria. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 3 – Metabolic Processes and Energy Transfers in Living Organisms
textbook_ref.subject: Biology

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a content of the lymphatic system?
explanation_steps: Lymph is tissue fluid drained into lymph vessels; it contains water, small proteins, lymphocytes and, in the lacteals, absorbed fats (G10 pp.85–87).
Red blood cells stay inside the blood capillaries. Answer: D.

similar_questions.stem: The lymph vessels in the villi that absorb fats are called
explanation_steps: Lacteals absorb fatty acids and glycerol (as fat droplets) into the lymph. Answer: B.

questions.stem: One of the following sequences represent a flow of air from the environment to the human body.

options.A: Nasal cavity → pharynx → trachea → bronchioles and alveoli
options.B: Nasal cavity → pharynx → larynx → lung and alveoli
options.C: Lung → pharynx → trachea and nasal cavity
options.D: Alveoli → lung → pharynx → nostrils and oral cavity
options.E: Nostril → alveoli → larynx → pharynx and lung

explanation_steps: Air pathway (G10 pp.109–110): nostrils → nasal cavity → pharynx → larynx → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli.

A lists the stages in the right order (it omits the larynx and bronchi). B is also in the right order (it omits the trachea and bronchi), so B is accepted too; C, D and E run in the wrong direction or jump about. A is keyed as the more complete path down to the alveoli.

similar_questions.stem: Which structure contains the vocal cords?
explanation_steps: The larynx (voice box) contains the vocal cords. Answer: B.

questions.review_flag: Both A (nasal cavity→pharynx→trachea→bronchioles and alveoli) and B (nasal cavity→pharynx→larynx→lung and alveoli) are correctly ordered but incomplete; A keyed, B accepted. Teacher to decide.

questions.stem: Lymphatic region located in the armpits that drains lymph from the breasts is
explanation_steps: Lymph nodes are grouped in regions: cervical (neck), axillary (armpit – drains the arms and breasts), inguinal (groin), and nodes of the thoracic, abdominal and pelvic cavities (G10 p.90).
Answer: B.

similar_questions.stem: Lymph nodes in the neck belong to the
explanation_steps: Cervical = neck. Answer: C.

questions.stem: If a patient's urine contains sugar, then probably his/her ______ is damaged.
explanation_steps: Glucose in the urine is the classic sign of diabetes mellitus, caused by too little insulin from the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas; blood glucose rises above what the kidney tubules can reabsorb (G11 pp.17–18).
Answer: D. (Kidney damage more typically lets protein into the urine.)

similar_questions.stem: Insulin lowers blood glucose by

options.B: stimulating cells to take up glucose and the liver to store it as glycogen

explanation_steps: Insulin promotes glucose uptake and glycogen formation. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 1.3 Abnormal secretion of the pancreas – diabetes mellitus
textbook_ref.subject: Biology

questions.stem: Anaerobic respiration cannot occur in
explanation_steps: Anaerobic respiration releases energy without oxygen (G9 pp.132–133): yeast (alcoholic fermentation), many bacteria and protozoa, and human muscle cells during vigorous exercise (lactic acid fermentation).
It can occur in all of them. Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: The product of anaerobic respiration in human muscles is
explanation_steps: Glucose → lactic acid + small amount of energy. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 3 – Metabolic Processes and Energy Transfers in Living Organisms
textbook_ref.subject: Biology

questions.stem: All of the following are parts of the ear, except
explanation_steps: The choroid is the pigmented, vascular middle layer of the eye (G10 p.148).
The ossicles (malleus, incus, stapes) are in the middle ear and the vestibule is part of the inner ear (G10 pp.155–156). Answer: A.

similar_questions.stem: The part of the inner ear concerned with hearing is the
explanation_steps: The cochlea contains the hearing receptors; the semicircular canals are for balance. Answer: B.

questions.stem: The structure of neuron which is responsible to transmit electrochemical signals from one neuron to the other is
explanation_steps: Dendrites carry impulses towards the cell body; the axon carries impulses away from the cell body to the next neuron (across a synapse) or to an effector (G10 pp.165–167).
Answer: B. (The myelin sheath insulates the axon and speeds conduction.)

similar_questions.stem: The junction between two neurons is called a
explanation_steps: Impulses cross the synapse by neurotransmitters. Answer: B.

questions.review_flag: Option D is printed 'mylen sheath' (myelin sheath).

questions.stem: One of the following processes does not occur in a female's reproductive system.
explanation_steps: Spermatogenesis (sperm formation) takes place in the seminiferous tubules of the male testes (G11 pp.28–31).
Oogenesis, ovulation and menstruation occur in the female system, and fertilisation takes place in the oviduct. Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: The release of a mature egg from the ovary is called
explanation_steps: Ovulation happens around day 14 of the menstrual cycle. Answer: C.

questions.stem: The function that is not done by voluntary muscles is
explanation_steps: Voluntary (skeletal) muscles move the skeleton, maintain posture, make facial expressions and move the ribs and diaphragm in breathing (G11 pp.74–76).
Peristalsis is done by involuntary smooth muscle in the wall of the gut. Answer: D.

similar_questions.stem: Which type of muscle never tires and is found only in the heart?
explanation_steps: Cardiac muscle contracts rhythmically throughout life. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Cartilage is part of all the following structures, except
explanation_steps: Textbook (G11 p.57): 'the ear lobes and parts of the larynx are made of cartilage. Cartilage joins the ends of the ribs to the sternum and covers the ends of bones. It forms the lining of the trachea.'
The skull (cranium) is made of bone joined by immovable sutures. Answer: D.
Note: anatomically the soft earlobe (lobule) itself has no cartilage – the cartilage is in the rest of the pinna – but the paper follows the textbook wording.

similar_questions.stem: Cartilage is gradually replaced by bone during development in a process called
explanation_steps: Ossification converts the cartilage skeleton of the fetus into bone. Answer: B.

questions.stem: One of the following steps is not part of translation.
explanation_steps: Translation (protein synthesis at the ribosome) has initiation (the ribosome assembles on the mRNA with the first tRNA), elongation (amino acids are added) and termination (a stop codon releases the chain) (G12 pp.12–14).
RNA synthesis is transcription, which happens before translation, in the nucleus. Answer: A.

similar_questions.stem: During translation, the anticodon is found on
explanation_steps: tRNA carries the anticodon that pairs with the mRNA codon. Answer: C.

questions.stem: The theory of "natural selection" considers all of the following factors, except
explanation_steps: Textbook (G12 p.63): Darwin's theory of natural selection considers overproduction (fecundity), variation, struggle for existence, survival of the fittest and inheritance.
Darwin could not explain the source of variation; mutation was added later by Neo-Darwinism (the synthetic theory). Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: Neo-Darwinism combines Darwin's natural selection with
explanation_steps: The synthetic theory adds modern genetics to natural selection. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Genetic isolation due to incompatibility of the reproductive structure of individuals is known as ______ isolation.
explanation_steps: Mechanical isolation: the reproductive organs (genitalia or flower parts) of two species do not fit, so mating or pollination cannot take place (G12 pp.83–84).
Gametic isolation is when gametes meet but cannot fuse. Answer: B.

similar_questions.stem: Two frog species breed in the same pond but one breeds in March and the other in June. This is
explanation_steps: Different breeding times = seasonal isolation. Answer: B.

questions.stem: The phosphorus cycle is essential to add phosphorus to life molecules such as
explanation_steps: Phosphorus, released by the weathering of rocks, is taken up by plants and built into phosphate groups of nucleotides – DNA and RNA – as well as ATP and phospholipids (G12 pp.98–100).
Carbohydrates (C, H, O) and proteins (C, H, O, N, S) do not normally contain phosphorus. Answer: D.

similar_questions.stem: The main natural reservoir of phosphorus is
explanation_steps: Unlike carbon and nitrogen, phosphorus has no significant gas phase; it is stored in rocks. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Monohybrid cross between homozygous tall plant with a short plant (Tall = T and short = t) produces an offspring with the following genotype.
explanation_steps: TT × tt: every gamete of the tall parent carries T and every gamete of the short parent carries t (G12 pp.29–32).
All F₁ offspring are Tt (100%), and all are tall. Answer: C.

similar_questions.stem: Two Tt plants are crossed. What fraction of the offspring is expected to be short (tt)?
explanation_steps: Tt × Tt → 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt, so 1/4 are tt (short).

questions.stem: The central part of an atom is called a (n)
explanation_steps: An atom has a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus at its centre (protons and neutrons), surrounded by electrons (G9 pp.43–44).
Answer: D.

similar_questions.stem: Who discovered the nucleus with the gold-foil (alpha scattering) experiment?
explanation_steps: Rutherford (1911) concluded that the mass and positive charge are concentrated in a small nucleus. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 2 – Atomic Structure and Chemical Bonding
textbook_ref.subject: Chemistry

questions.stem: Which of the following is a metallic element?
explanation_steps: Calcium is a group IIA (alkaline earth) metal (G9 p.23; G10 p.15).
Bromine and chlorine are halogens (non-metals); oxygen and nitrogen are non-metallic gases. Answer: B.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is a non-metal?
explanation_steps: Sulphur is a brittle yellow non-metal. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 1 – Chemistry: The Study of Matter
textbook_ref.subject: Chemistry

questions.stem: The chemical symbol for the metallic element which exists in the liquid state at room temperature is
explanation_steps: Mercury is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature; its symbol Hg comes from the Latin 'hydrargyrum' (G9 pp.23, 82).
Ag – silver, Au – gold, Pb – lead, Sn – tin (all solids). Answer: D.

similar_questions.stem: The symbol of lead is Pb, from its Latin name
explanation_steps: Plumbum → Pb (tin = stannum → Sn). Answer: A.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 3 – Chemical Symbols, Formulas and Equations
textbook_ref.section: 3.1 Chemical symbols – symbols from Latin names
textbook_ref.subject: Chemistry

questions.stem: Which of the following scientists arranged elements on the bases of their atomic numbers?
explanation_steps: Henry Moseley (1913) used X-ray spectra to find atomic numbers and showed that the periodic properties depend on atomic number – the modern periodic law (G10 p.16).
Döbereiner (triads), Newlands (octaves) and Mendeleev all arranged elements by atomic mass. Answer: C.

similar_questions.stem: Mendeleev arranged the elements in order of increasing
explanation_steps: Mendeleev's periodic law (1869) was based on atomic mass. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 1.1 Development of the periodic table – Moseley
textbook_ref.subject: Chemistry

questions.stem: The type of acid, which is useful for the digestion of food, is
explanation_steps: Uses of common acids (G10 p.123): hydrochloric acid in the gastric juice of the stomach helps the digestion of food (it activates pepsin and kills germs).
Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: Which acid is found in car batteries?
explanation_steps: Lead–acid batteries contain dilute sulphuric acid. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Carbon has an atomic number of
explanation_steps: Carbon has 6 protons, so Z = 6 (electron configuration 2, 4) (G9 p.44).
12 is its mass number (¹²₆C); 7 is nitrogen and 8 is oxygen. Answer: B.

similar_questions.stem: How many valence electrons does a carbon atom have?
explanation_steps: Z = 6 → 2, 4: four electrons in the outer shell.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 2 – Atomic Structure and Chemical Bonding
textbook_ref.subject: Chemistry

similar_questions.stem: How many calories are in 836.8 J? [1 cal = 4.184 J]

textbook_ref.section: 5.1 Units of heat energy – calorie and joule
textbook_ref.subject: Chemistry

questions.review_flag: Exact value 41.84 J; option D (42 J) uses the rounded 1 cal ≈ 4.2 J.

questions.stem: The rate of a reaction can be measured by the change in its
explanation_steps: Textbook (G11 p.2): the rate of reaction can be followed by measuring a change in mass or gas volume, a change in colour, a change in pH, the change in temperature or the change in conductivity.
All four are listed. Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: Which unit could be used for the rate of a reaction?
explanation_steps: Rate = change in concentration / time → mol/L per second. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 1 – Rate of a Chemical Reaction and Factors Affecting it
textbook_ref.subject: Chemistry

questions.stem: The oxidation state of manganese in MnO₄⁻ ion is
explanation_steps: The sum of oxidation numbers in an ion equals its charge; O = −2 (G11 p.31).
x + 4(−2) = −1 → x = +7. Answer: D. (+6 is the value in MnO₄²⁻, manganate.)

similar_questions.stem: What is the oxidation number of Cr in Cr₂O₇²⁻?

questions.stem: The most abundant substance in the atmosphere is
explanation_steps: Dry air is about 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, 0.9% argon and 0.04% carbon dioxide by volume (G11 p.86).
Answer: C.

similar_questions.stem: Approximately what percentage of air by volume is oxygen?
explanation_steps: About 21% (one-fifth). Answer: B.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 3 – Chemistry of Some Nonmetals and Their Compounds
textbook_ref.subject: Chemistry

questions.stem: ______ is an alloy of iron.
explanation_steps: Steel is iron with a small amount of carbon (and other metals) (G9 p.26; G10 p.64).
Solder = tin + lead; bronze = copper + tin; brass = copper + zinc; duralumin = aluminium + copper (+ Mg, Mn). Answer: B.

similar_questions.stem: Brass is an alloy of
explanation_steps: Brass = Cu + Zn. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 1 – Chemistry: The Study of Matter
textbook_ref.subject: Chemistry

questions.stem: Which of the following properties are considered measurable properties of gases?
explanation_steps: The state of a gas is described by four measurable variables: pressure P, volume V, temperature T and amount n (moles), related by the gas laws (PV = nRT) (Chemistry G11 Unit 5).
Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: At constant temperature, a gas has a volume of 2.0 L at 1.0 atm. What is its volume at 4.0 atm?
explanation_steps: Boyle's law: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂ → V₂ = 1.0 × 2.0 / 4.0 = 0.50 L.

textbook_ref.note: Grade 11 Unit 5 (Behaviour of Gases, printed pp.162-190) is missing from the supplied PDF (it ends at p.129); page taken from the book's table of contents, text not verified.
textbook_ref.subject: Chemistry

questions.stem: The number of atoms bonded to a central atom in a linear molecular geometry are
explanation_steps: In VSEPR theory a linear molecule has two atoms (bonding domains) around the central atom at 180°, e.g. BeCl₂, CO₂ (G12 pp.6–8).
Trigonal planar = 3, tetrahedral = 4, trigonal bipyramidal = 5, octahedral = 6. Answer: B.

similar_questions.stem: What is the shape of BF₃?

questions.stem: Which of the following is a vector quantity?

explanation_steps: Rules (G9 pp.34–37): leading zeros are not significant; zeros between non-zero digits are significant; trailing zeros after the decimal point are significant.

tips: Write it in scientific notation: 4.050 × 10⁻² – every digit shown is significant.

similar_questions.stem: How many significant figures are in 2.0300?

questions.stem: A man walks 70 m West, then 130 m East, and then 80 m South. What is the magnitude of the total displacement?

The two components are perpendicular: d = √(60² + 80²) = √(3600 + 6400) = √10000 = 100 m. Answer: C. (280 m is the total distance walked.)

similar_questions.stem: A girl walks 50 m North, 20 m South and then 40 m East. What is the magnitude of her displacement?
explanation_steps: Net north = 30 m, east = 40 m; d = √(30² + 40²) = 50 m.

questions.stem: A uniformly accelerated motion has a constant
explanation_steps: In uniformly accelerated motion the velocity changes by equal amounts in equal time intervals, so the acceleration is constant (G9 pp.81–82).
Because velocity changes, speed, momentum (mv) and kinetic energy also change. Answer: D.

questions.stem: A body is sliding down an inclined plane having a coefficient of friction of 0.5. If the normal force is twice the net force along the incline, the angle between the incline and the horizontal is
questions.image_alt: Table 'Constants that you may require for questions 71-100': acceleration due to gravity g = 10 m/s²; velocity of light in air and free space c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s; refractive index of air n(air) ≈ 1; elementary charge e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C; Planck's constant h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s; sin 30° = cos 60° = 0.50; sin 45° = cos 45° = 0.71.
explanation_steps: On an incline of angle θ: normal force N = mg cos θ; net force down the incline F = mg sin θ − μ mg cos θ (G9 pp.177–181).
N = 2F → mg cos θ = 2(mg sin θ − 0.5 mg cos θ) = 2mg sin θ − mg cos θ → 2 cos θ = 2 sin θ → tan θ = 1.
θ = 45°. Answer: C. (Check with sin 45° = cos 45° = 0.71: F = 0.71mg − 0.355mg = 0.355mg and N = 0.71mg = 2F ✓.)

questions.stem: Figure 1 represents the trajectory of a projectile going from A to E. Air resistance is negligible. Which of the following is wrong? [Figure 1: launch point A and landing point E on the same horizontal level; B on the way up, C the highest point, D on the way down]
questions.image_alt: Figure 1: the parabolic trajectory of a projectile above a horizontal line. It is launched at A (on the ground, left), rises through B, reaches its highest point C, descends through D and lands at E (on the ground, right, at the same level as A).

options.A: The speed is lowest at point C.
options.B: The speed is greatest at points A and E.
options.C: The speed is the same at points A and E.
options.D: The velocity is the same at points A and E.
options.E: The acceleration is the same at points B and C.

explanation_steps: Without air resistance the horizontal velocity is constant and the vertical velocity changes at g. At C the vertical velocity is zero, so the speed is lowest there (A true); A and E are at the same height, so the speeds there are equal and greatest (B, C true) (G10 pp.8–12).
The acceleration is g downward everywhere (E true).
At A the velocity points upward and at E it points downward, so the velocities are NOT the same (only their magnitudes are). D is wrong. Answer: D.
tips: Same speed ≠ same velocity: velocity includes direction.

similar_questions.stem: At the highest point of a projectile's path, which quantity is zero?
explanation_steps: Only the vertical component of velocity is zero at the top; the horizontal velocity and g remain. Answer: B.

questions.stem: What is the name of a thermodynamic process in which no heat is transferred?
explanation_steps: Adiabatic process: Q = 0, no heat enters or leaves the system (G10 pp.94–95). Isothermal = constant temperature; isobaric = constant pressure; isochoric = constant volume.
E is keyed. B is also accepted: an isentropic process is a reversible adiabatic process, so it too involves no heat transfer (the term is not in the textbook).

similar_questions.stem: In an isothermal expansion of an ideal gas, which quantity stays constant?
explanation_steps: Isothermal = constant temperature (so ΔU = 0 and Q = W). Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is wrong?

options.A: In a plane mirror, the object and image distances are equal.
options.B: The image formed by a plane mirror is real image.
options.C: The magnification of a plane mirror is 1.

options.E: The size of the object and size of the image formed by a plane mirror are equal.

explanation_steps: A plane mirror forms a virtual, upright image of the same size, as far behind the mirror as the object is in front (G10 pp.223–226).
The reflected rays only appear to come from the image, which cannot be caught on a screen, so the image is virtual, not real. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Sound waves are mechanical and cannot travel through
explanation_steps: Sound is a mechanical wave: it needs a material medium (solid, liquid or gas) whose particles vibrate (G11 pp.182–184).
There are no particles in a vacuum, so sound cannot travel through it (the bell-jar experiment). Answer: D.

similar_questions.stem: In which medium does sound travel fastest?
explanation_steps: Sound is fastest in solids such as steel (about 5000 m/s). Answer: D.

questions.stem: A wave in which the particles of the medium move in a direction parallel to the direction that the wave moves is a
explanation_steps: Longitudinal waves (e.g. sound) have particle vibrations parallel to the direction of travel, forming compressions and rarefactions; in transverse waves the vibrations are perpendicular (G11 pp.149–150).
Answer: A.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is a transverse wave?
explanation_steps: Light (an electromagnetic wave) is transverse. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 3.1 Types of waves – longitudinal and transverse
textbook_ref.subject: Physics

questions.stem: In addition to the three states of matter (solid, liquid and gas), the fourth state of matter is
explanation_steps: Textbook (G12 p.2): 'In addition to the three states of matter, the fourth state of matter, plasma – a highly ionized state of matter' (found in stars, lightning and fluorescent lamps).
Answer: B.

similar_questions.stem: Liquids and gases are both called fluids because they
explanation_steps: A fluid is any substance that can flow. Answer: B.

questions.stem: A camel weighs 1200 kg. The area of each foot of the camel is 400 cm². If the weight of the camel is evenly distributed amongst the feet, the pressure acting on each foot, in pascals, is [g = 10 m/s²]
questions.image_alt: Table 'Constants that you may require for questions 71-100': acceleration due to gravity g = 10 m/s²; velocity of light in air and free space c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s; refractive index of air n(air) ≈ 1; elementary charge e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C; Planck's constant h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s; sin 30° = cos 60° = 0.50; sin 45° = cos 45° = 0.71.
explanation_steps: Weight W = mg = 1200 × 10 = 12 000 N, shared equally by 4 feet → 3000 N per foot (G12 pp.11–13).
Area of one foot = 400 cm² = 0.04 m². p = F/A = 3000 / 0.04 = 75 000 Pa. Answer: D. (The same result follows from 12 000 N / 0.16 m².)
tips: Convert cm² to m²: divide by 10 000.

similar_questions.stem: A 60 kg woman stands on one heel of area 1 cm². What pressure does she exert? [g = 10 m/s²]

questions.review_flag: 'Weighs 1200 kg' gives a mass, not a weight; the weight is 12 000 N with g = 10 m/s². The item assumes 4 feet.

questions.stem: According to pascal's principle, if an external force causes an increase in pressure at any point in a confined incompressible fluid, every point in the fluid experiences
explanation_steps: Pascal's principle: pressure applied to an enclosed incompressible fluid is transmitted undiminished to every part of the fluid and the container walls (G12 pp.51–55).
Answer: B.

similar_questions.stem: Which device works on Pascal's principle?
explanation_steps: Hydraulic brakes, lifts and presses transmit pressure through a liquid. Answer: B.

questions.stem: The true nature of light includes both wave and particle characteristics. This character of light is a
explanation_steps: Wave–particle duality: light shows wave properties (interference, diffraction) and particle properties (photons in the photoelectric effect) (G12 pp.91, 99).
Answer: B.

similar_questions.stem: Which phenomenon shows the particle nature of light?
explanation_steps: The photoelectric effect can only be explained with photons. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Photocell is a device used to convert light energy into
explanation_steps: A photocell (photoelectric cell) uses the photoelectric effect: light falling on a cathode releases electrons, producing an electric current (G12 pp.116–118).
Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following uses a photocell?
explanation_steps: Interrupting the light beam changes the photocurrent and triggers the circuit. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 2.4 Applications of the photoelectric effect – photocell
textbook_ref.subject: Physics

questions.stem: The frequency of a light photon is 5 × 10¹⁸ Hz. The energy of the light in joules is [h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s]
questions.image_alt: Table 'Constants that you may require for questions 71-100': acceleration due to gravity g = 10 m/s²; velocity of light in air and free space c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s; refractive index of air n(air) ≈ 1; elementary charge e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C; Planck's constant h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s; sin 30° = cos 60° = 0.50; sin 45° = cos 45° = 0.71.
explanation_steps: Photon energy E = hf (G12 pp.100–102).
E = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 5 × 10¹⁸ = 3.315 × 10⁻¹⁵ ≈ 3.32 × 10⁻¹⁵ J. Answer: A. (Such a high frequency is in the X-ray region.)

similar_questions.stem: What is the energy of a photon of wavelength 600 nm? [h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s, c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s]

questions.review_flag: The frequency is printed '5 × 1018 Hz' (superscript lost); read as 5 × 10¹⁸ Hz, which gives option A exactly. Option E (15.5 nm) is not an energy.
